--- title: "[Graph.rescale_node_attrs()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Rescale node attribute values to a range. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19403-L19583){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.rescale_node_attrs( node_attr_from=None, values=None, node_attr_to="size", range=None, nodes=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Rescale node attributes](/assets/graphs/rescale-node-attrs.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Before: a six-node graph whose nodes carry raw scores from 0 to 10, shown as badges, all drawn at one size. After: the scores are rescaled linearly into the default range 0.5 to 1.0 and written as each node's size, so F becomes 0.5 and B 1.0, with every node drawn in proportion." width="100%"} Linearly maps numeric node values onto a target interval and writes the results to another node attribute, `size` by default, modifying the graph in place. The smallest input value maps to the lower end of `range=`, the largest to the upper end, and everything else proportionally in between (min-max scaling). The source attribute is not changed. This is mainly used to turn analysis results into visual encodings, for example: - sizing nodes by centrality, degree, or PageRank so important nodes stand out - putting measures with very different scales onto a common interval before comparing or combining them - producing an inverted scale (large values -> small output) by giving a reversed range Only the minimum and maximum of the values matter, so a single outlier can compress every other node toward one end of the range. If all values are equal, every node receives the lower bound of `range=`. Values must be numeric; non-numeric values raise a `TypeError`. The mapping is recorded on the graph and listed under "Node aesthetics" by `describe()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_attr_from]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the numeric node attribute to read (e.g., `"betweenness_centrality"`, `"score"`). Nodes without this attribute are left unchanged. Ignored for reading when `values=` is given (it is then only used to label the recorded aesthetic). Default is `None`; either this or `values=` must be supplied. [values]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[str, int | float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A dict mapping nodes to numeric values, keyed by node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). Use this to rescale data that isn't stored as an attribute, such as the output of a `return_dict=True` computation. If given, it takes precedence over `node_attr_from=` and `nodes=`. Default is `None`. [node_attr_to]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["size"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute that receives the rescaled values. Default is `"size"`, which the interactive graph widget uses for node size. Existing values in this attribute are overwritten for the rescaled nodes. Writing back to the same name as `node_attr_from=` replaces the original values. [range]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A two-element list `[low, high]` giving the output interval. Default is `None`, which means `[0.5, 1.0]`. Sizes within `[0, 1]` are treated by the graph widget as relative values and scaled to pixels, while larger numbers are used as given. If `low` is greater than `high`, the scale is inverted. [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[list[str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A list of node IDs or labels restricting which nodes are read from `node_attr_from=`. The minimum and maximum are then computed over these nodes only. If `None` (the default), all nodes are considered. Ignored when `values=` is given. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If neither `node_attr_from=` nor `values=` is provided, or if `range=` does not contain exactly two values. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Rescaling a stored attribute with the default settings writes values between `0.5` and `1.0` to `size`. The lowest score (`B`, 2) maps to `0.5`, the highest (`C`, 10) maps to `1.0`, and `A` (6) lands halfway: ::: {#fe10fafb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec G = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes({"A": {"score": 6}, "B": {"score": 2}, "C": {"score": 10}}) ) G.rescale_node_attrs(node_attr_from="score") G.get_node_df().select("label", "score", "size") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 3)
labelscoresize
stri64f64
"A"60.75
"B"20.5
"C"101.0
``` ::: ::: Results returned by analysis methods can be passed via `values=`. Rescaling betweenness centrality on a 5-node path into `[5, 20]` makes the middle node the largest and the two endpoints the smallest: ::: {#bba2654b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} G = ec.Graph() G.add_nodes(range(5)) G.add_edges([("0", "1"), ("1", "2"), ("2", "3"), ("3", "4")]) betweenness = G.betweenness_centrality(return_dict=True) G.rescale_node_attrs(values=betweenness, node_attr_to="size", range=[5, 20]) G.get_node_attrs("size") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {3: 20.0, 1: 5.0, 5: 5.0, 4: 16.25, 2: 16.25} ``` ::: ::: A reversed range inverts the scale. Here the node with the most neighbors (the hub, `0`) gets the smallest `width`, and the three leaves get the largest: ::: {#e15d6e78 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} G = ec.Graph() G.add_nodes(range(4)) G.add_edges([("0", "1"), ("0", "2"), ("0", "3")]) degrees = {n: len(G.neighbors(node=n)) for n in G.get_node_ids(limit=None)} G.rescale_node_attrs(values=degrees, node_attr_to="width", range=[10, 1]) G.get_node_attrs("width") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {3: 10.0, 1: 1.0, 4: 10.0, 2: 10.0} ``` ::: :::
